text:
Happy Thursday! We're starting cloudy and chilly, right around 40, and the dry start won't last. Rain moves in around noon and is steadiest from about 1 to 5. It's a light one, a tenth of an inch at most, so think umbrella weather rather than a washout. The high is near 41. The models disagree on how wet this gets, with one much drier than the other two. I'd lean toward the wetter side and keep the umbrella handy.

Tonight the rain fades to a mix of rain and wet snow, with a low around 32. Burlington should stay just above freezing, so the most you'll see is some slush on grassy spots, and the roads should be fine. A few flakes could linger before 9 Friday morning. After that it's cloudy and mostly dry with a high near 42. Saturday morning is the coldest of the stretch, in the 20s, so expect frost on the windshield. Next week looks dry and milder, with 50s possible by midweek.

AFD DISCUSSION (the forecaster's full reasoning, same regional caveat; their temps are area-wide ranges):
KEY MESSAGE 1: A gradually deepening surface low will track from the Ohio Valley east over southern New England before heading off into the Canadian Maritimes today into tomorrow. Despite a favorable storm track for snow, a marginally cold airmass will be in place at the onset, especially at the surface due to a lack of Canadian high pressure to the north. Precipitation will enter southwestern areas this morning but very slowly make its way northeast during the day. By tonight, it should reach the Northeast Kingdom, but the heaviest rates will remain to the south. It will likely never reach the St. Lawrence Valley though. At the onset, surface temperatures will be in the 30s in most places, with low 40s in the warmest valleys. Steep lapse rates will exist with summit levels well below freezing, though a lack of a significantly dry layer will prevent significant wet-bulb cooling. Precipitation will begin as rain in the valleys and snow at the summits. An estimate of initial snow levels is around 1,500 ft. Light rates and daytime occurrence will prevent significant accumulations at the onset outside the mountains. A weak November sun angle will limit some of the warming effects though. Heading into tonight, heavier rates should enter southern areas, and darkness will end any solar radiation. The combination of lowering temperatures due to dynamical cooling and nighttime cooling will allow snow levels to drop a bit, and especially allow for more efficient accumulations at higher elevations with higher snow ratios. By Friday morning, snow levels should be around or below 1,000 ft. While brief periods of snow are possible in the low valleys like the Champlain Valley and the Lower Connecticut Valley, temperatures will likely stay just above freezing and prevent accumulations other than maybe some slush on grassy-type surfaces. As the low tracks to the east heading through Friday, cyclonic northwest flow will develop and maintain periods of upslope snow showers in the higher terrain through Saturday. Boundary layer temperatures will reach their lowest values Saturday morning, with most areas likely seeing temperatures in the 20s. However, that time period will likely be dry and prevent any snow from occurring in the valleys. Warm Lake Champlain temperatures will probably further limit the already marginal accumulations in the immediate Champlain Valley, especially with northwest flow off the lake and downsloping along the eastern Adirondacks. Confidence has increased in a more southerly storm track and a less impactful event. Our deterministic most-likely scenario has snow amounts in the 2-5 inch range for the southern Adirondacks, central Greens and southern Greens around and above 2,000 ft. Areas between 1,000-2,000 ft look to be in the 0-2 inch range, and below 1,000 ft looks to be a slushy coating at most. WCAX METEOROLOGIST (regional station — Burlington relevance only, never their branding): BURLINGTON, Vt. (WCAX) -Happy Thursday! Our Thursday starts dry early on, but mixed rain showers and mountain snow showers start to make their arrival from south to north into this morning. Right now, it looks like the bulk of the moisture is across southern and central portions of the area while areas further north stay mainly dry. Temperatures for the day are in the low to mid 40s. As cooler air starts to push in through this evening and tonight we begin to see a transition over from leftover rain to all snow. Again, the bulk of the snow will be across central and southern portions of the area. Overnight lows fall back into the 30s. Leftover snow showers continue into the start of the day Friday across central and southern portions of the area but begin to taper through the late morning and into the early afternoon. Our overall thinking for accumulation has not changed all that much. The mountain peaks of southern Vermont could run upwards of 6″ of new snow, but the totals quickly decline heading away from the mountains towards the Rt. 7 & I-91 corridors to only about a coating for those areas. If there was to be a slick morning commute it would likely be Friday morning in some of the mountain passes of central and southern Vermont and Rt. 4 and Rt. 9 trekking west and east through the mountains. We are drier through Friday afternoon with highs in the 30s to about 40. This upcoming weekend could feature the chance for a few more mountain snow showers and valley rain showers for Saturday and Sunday, but accumulation at this point does not look all that substantial. Temperatures for both days are in the 30s to about 40s. Into the next week we trend drier and warmer, as more sunshine emerges helping to push our temperatures into the low to mid 40s Monday, and even back into the 50s by Tuesday and Wednesday.
NBC5 METEOROLOGIST (2026-11-11T22:09:00Z — same caveat): Rain and elevation snow slowly fill in throughout Thursday — Rain and elevation snow showers develop Thursday, especially by afternoon, as an area of low pressure approaches. A period of steadier rain and mountain snow is likely Thursday night into Friday, with sprinkles and flurries lingering into Saturday. Several inches of snow will fall in southern parts of the region, higher up. Drier and brighter weather is likely next week, followed by a warmup into the 50s.
